15: # Hermes Hook Contract
16: 
17: Hermes has two hook surfaces. One is the operator's; one the repo can carry.
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: Hermes keeps shell hooks in the operator's user-level config and reads a repo plugin from `.hermes/plugins/`. This reference records both surfaces and the plugin hook map that carries the repo's guard cores into a Hermes session.
22: 
23: ---
24: 
25: ## 2. SHELL HOOKS (USER-LEVEL)
26: 
27: Shell-script hooks are declared under `hooks:` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`, gated by a per-command consent allowlist at `~/.hermes/shell-hooks-allowlist.json`, and inspected with `hermes hooks list|test|doctor`. `--accept-hooks` or `HERMES_ACCEPT_HOOKS=1` bypasses the consent prompt on a headless run, and `hermes -z` sets it automatically.
28: 
29: The repo cannot declare these. None is configured on this machine (observed 2026-09-14: `hooks:` absent, `~/.hermes/hooks/` empty). A dispatch never passes `--accept-hooks` unless the operator declared hooks and asked for it.
30: 
31: ---
32: 
33: ## 3. PROJECT PLUGIN (REPO-CARRIABLE)
34: 
35: Native plugins load from `./.hermes/plugins/<name>/` when `HERMES_ENABLE_PROJECT_PLUGINS` is set, and their hook list covers every guard core this repo runs (source-read: `hermes_cli/plugins.py`). The hook-and-plugin phase builds `.hermes/plugins/repo-guards/`, which re-implements nothing: each hook shells out to the existing `.mjs` or `.sh` core under `.skilled/hooks/` and maps its result to Hermes's block-or-continue contract, failing open on a core error as the `.pi/extensions/` adapters do.
36: 
37: | Hermes hook | Repo guard core | Effect |
38: |---|---|---|
39: | `pre_llm_call` | skill advisor CLI; spec-gate classifier | Appends the advisor brief every turn and classifies the prompt for the Gate 3 spec-folder gate; the question itself is delivered at the first mutation, not on the turn; the classification is skipped for an orchestrated leaf |
40: | `pre_tool_call` | self-dispatch refusal; read-only refusal; spec-gate enforcement; dispatch preflight lint; task-dispatch guard; MCP route guard; sk-git advisory | Refuses a nested `hermes chat`; refuses the write and command tools when `SPECKIT_HERMES_READ_ONLY=1`; blocks a `write_file` or `patch` the enforced spec gate has not been bound for yet; blocks a `cli-*` dispatch or a `delegate_task` the guards reject; stages the sk-git and MCP-route advisories |
41: | `transform_tool_result` | the Gate 3 notice for an un-enforced write; the staged advisories; post-edit quality | Appends the Gate 3 notice to the first write of an open-gate session, the staged advisories, and the post-edit quality warning for `write_file` and `patch` (the core runs here because post and transform hooks run on separate bounded threads) |
42: | `on_session_start` | shared goal core | Binds the packet named by `HERMES_SPEC_FOLDER` to the session id |
43: | `pre_verify` | completion-evidence stop | Returns a continue nudge when a completion claim names no evidence |
44: | system prompt sections | session-start context; persona; goal core; session-start guards | Four sections under the 4000-character cap: context, `agent-<name>` persona binding, the core's goal (else the packet slice), and the worktree, dist-freshness, git-hooks and primary-reconcile warnings |
45: | `on_session_end` | session-stop context; session cleanup | Records the closing state and reaps the MCP helpers the process spawned |
46: 
47: Validation: `hermes plugins validate ./.hermes/plugins/repo-guards` and `hermes plugins doctor`. Agent Plugins v1 portable packages exist in Hermes but are deferred here; their hook surface is unsettled.
48: 
49: ---
50: 
51: ## 4. WHAT A DISPATCH ASSUMES
52: 
53: The project plugin `repo-guards` (`.hermes/plugins/repo-guards/`) carries the repo guards into a Hermes session when `HERMES_ENABLE_PROJECT_PLUGINS=1` is set and `repo-guards` is listed under `plugins.enabled`; without both, a Hermes dispatch runs with no repo guard hooks. The prompt's preamble and the runtime's dispatch stack are the guards. The packet's hard rule `hooks-user-level` states the boundary so nobody claims otherwise.

13: 
14: # Skill Reference File Templates - AI Agent Skills
15: 
16: Templates for creating reference files in AI agent skills with deep-dive technical guidance.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Location & Naming
23: 
24: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/references/`
25: 
26: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only
27: 
28: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
29: |---------------|-----------------|
30: | `implementation-workflows.md` | `ImplementationWorkflows.md` (PascalCase) |
31: | `tool-catalog.md` | `tool_catalog.md` (snake_case) |
32: | `debugging-guide.md` | `DebuggingGuide.MD` (wrong case) |
33: | `quick-reference.md` | `quickReference.md` (camelCase) |
34: | `code-quality-standards.md` | `code quality standards.md` (spaces) |
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
69: 
70: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
72: 
73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74: 
75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```
95: 
96: #### BAD Intro Structure (duplicates content)
97: 
98: ```markdown
99: # Git Commit Workflows
100: 
101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
102: 
103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
104: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
105: 
106: ### When to Use      ← WRONG: This belongs in Section 1!
107: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: \## 1. OVERVIEW
112: 
113: ### Purpose
114: Provides systematic workflows...  ← Now this duplicates the intro!
115: 
116: ### Core Principle
117: Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!
118: ```
119: 
120: #### Intro vs Section 1 Content Placement
121: 
122: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | Section 1 OVERVIEW |
123: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
124: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat) |
125: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
126: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
127: | Primary Sources       | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (as "Key Sources") |
128: | Purpose (detailed)    | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
129: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
130: | Any H3 subsections    | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES              |
131: 
132: ---
133: 
134: ### Reference Body Skeleton
135: 
136: **Every reference body follows this order.** The hook and the Purpose say different things: the hook names the job, and the Purpose names the outcome.
137: 
138: ```markdown
139: # [Title]
140: 
141: [1-2 sentence hook: what this reference covers and when to reach for it.]
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 1. OVERVIEW
146: 
147: ### Purpose
148: 
149: [The outcome this reference produces, in one or two sentences.]
150: 
151: ### When to Use
152: 
153: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
154: - [Second trigger]
155: 
156: ### Core Principle
157: 
158: [One-line statement that governs every rule below.]
159: 
160: ### Boundaries
161: 
162: - **In scope**: [What this reference owns]
163: - **Out of scope**: [What belongs in a sibling reference]
164: 
165: ### Key Sources
166: 
167: - [title](url) - [What the source establishes]
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 2. [CONTENT SECTION]
172: 
173: ### [Rule Group]
174: 
175: - **Rule:** [What to do]
176: - **Why:** [The failure it prevents]
177: - **Check:** [How to verify it]
178: 
179: ---
180: 
181: ## 3. [CONTENT SECTION]
182: 
183: [Body of the section]
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 4. RELATED RESOURCES
188: 
189: - [title](./sibling-reference.md) - [What the reader gets there]
190: ```
191: 
192: **Rules the skeleton encodes:**
193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.
194: - Content sections use integer numbers only: `## 2.`, `## 3.`, and so on.
195: - Rule fields are `- **Label:** text` bullets, never two bold labels on consecutive lines.
196: - Links are `[title](url)`, never a bare URL.
197: - Every `---` has a blank line above it, so a divider never turns the line above into a setext heading.
198: - A related section, when present, is the last H2.
199: 
200: ---
201: 
202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
203: 
204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
205: 
206: **Core Purpose**:
207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
208: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
209: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216: 
217: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```
229: 
230: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.
231: 
232: ---
233: 
234: ## 3. WHEN TO CREATE REFERENCE FILES
235: 
236: ### Create Reference File When
237: 
238: **Workflow Complexity**:
239: - Multi-phase workflows with validation checkpoints
240: - Decision trees with multiple branches
241: - Pattern libraries with 5+ variations
242: - Systematic debugging procedures
243: 
244: **Technical Depth**:
245: - Root cause analysis required
246: - Tool integration details (MCP, scripts)
247: - Before/after code transformations
248: - Common error patterns and fixes
249: 
250: **Size Threshold**:
251: - Content exceeds 200 lines
252: - Multiple related workflows
253: - Extensive troubleshooting needed
254: 
255: ### Keep in SKILL.md When
256: 
257: **Core Content**:
258: - Overview and "When to Use"
259: - High-level workflow (3-5 steps)
260: - Essential rules (ALWAYS/NEVER/ESCALATE IF)
261:   > **Note**: RULES sections in SKILL.md use ALL-CAPS H3 headers: `### ALWAYS`, `### NEVER`, `### ESCALATE IF` (or `####` at phase depth). See [skill-md-template.md](./skill-md-template.md) for the complete pattern.
262: - Quick reference
263: 
264: **Size**: Content under 200 lines
265: 
266: ### Reference File Types for AI Agent Skills
267: 
268: | Type                | Purpose                                | Example (kebab-case)          | Size           |
269: | ------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------- |
270: | **Workflow**        | Multi-phase processes with checkpoints | `implementation-workflows.md` | 500-1500 lines |
271: | **Pattern Library** | Code patterns with before/after        | `shared-patterns.md`          | 300-800 lines  |
272: | **Standards**       | Rules and conventions                  | `code-quality-standards.md`   | 400-1000 lines |
273: | **Debugging**       | Systematic troubleshooting             | `debugging-workflows.md`      | 600-1200 lines |
274: | **Tool Guide**      | MCP/external tool integration          | `devtools-guide.md`           | 200-600 lines  |
275: | **Quick Reference** | Commands, shortcuts, checklists        | `quick-reference.md`          | 200-400 lines  |
276: 
277: **Note:** All authored reference file names use kebab-case (hyphens, lowercase).
278: 
279: ---
280: 
281: ## 4. AI AGENT SKILL REFERENCE CHARACTERISTICS
282: 
283: ### Core Principle Statements
284: 
285: **Purpose**: Distill philosophy into one-line wisdom
286: 
287: > **PLACEMENT**: Core Principle goes in **Section 1 OVERVIEW**, NOT in the intro paragraph after the H1 title.
288: 
289: **Format**:
290: ```markdown
291: \## 1. OVERVIEW
292: 
293: ### Purpose
294: 
295: [The outcome this reference produces]
296: 
297: ### When to Use
298: 
299: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
300: 
301: ### Core Principle
302: 
303: [Single powerful statement that captures the workflow's essence]
304: ```
305: 
306: **Examples from Real Skills**:
307: - "Wait for the actual condition you care about, not a guess about how long it takes"
308: - "ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure"
309: - "Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history"
310: 
311: ### Phased Workflows with Validation
312: 
313: **Purpose**: Structured processes with mandatory checkpoints
314: 
315: **Format**:
316: ```markdown
317: ### The [Number] Phases
318: 
319: You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.
320: 
321: #### Phase 1: [Phase Name]
322: 
323: **Purpose**: [What this phase accomplishes]
324: 
325: **Actions**:
326: 1. [Action 1]
327: 2. [Action 2]
328: 
329: **Validation**: `checkpoint_name`
330: 
331: #### Phase 2: [Phase Name]
332: 
333: [Similar structure]
334: ```
335: 
336: **Key Elements**:
337: - **"You MUST complete"** - Mandatory language
338: - **Named checkpoints** - `checkpoint_name` for validation
339: - **Sequential phases** - Cannot skip ahead
340: 
341: ### Before/After Code Examples
342: 
343: **Purpose**: Show transformation from wrong to right
344: 
345: **Format**:
346: ```markdown
347: ### [Pattern Name]
348: 
349: **BEFORE**: [Problem description]
350: \```[language]
351: // Bad code with issues
352: // Showing what NOT to do
353: \```
354: 
355: **AFTER**: [Solution description]
356: \```[language]
357: // Good code with fixes
358: // Showing correct approach
359: \```
360: 
361: **Why better**: [Explanation of improvement]
362: ```
363: 
364: **Key Elements**:
365: - `BEFORE:` marker for the wrong-way code
366: - `AFTER:` marker for the right-way code
367: - Inline comments explaining issues
368: - "Why better" rationale
369: 
370: ### Pattern Comparison Tables
371: 
372: **Purpose**: Compare approaches across scenarios
373: 
374: **Format**:
375: ```markdown
376: ### Common Patterns
377: 
378: | Scenario     | Approach A (Wrong) | Approach B (Right) | Why Better  |
379: | ------------ | ------------------ | ------------------ | ----------- |
380: | [Scenario 1] | [Wrong way]        | [Right way]        | [Rationale] |
381: | [Scenario 2] | [Wrong way]        | [Right way]        | [Rationale] |
382: ```
383: 
384: **Use when**: Multiple scenarios need comparison
385: 
386: ### Decision Logic in Markdown
387: 
388: **Purpose**: Explicit if/then logic for workflow decisions
389: 
390: **Format**:
391: \```markdown
392: ### Decision Logic
393: 
394: \```markdown
395: IF [condition A]:
396:   → [Action/Path A]
397:   → [Expected outcome A]
398: 
399: IF [condition B]:
400:   → [Action/Path B]
401:   → [Expected outcome B]
402: 
403: IF [condition C]:
404:   → [Action/Path C]
405:   → [Expected outcome C]
406: \```
407: \```
408: 
409: **Alternative format** (decision tree):
410: \```markdown
411: \```
412: Analyze situation
413: ├─ Condition A met
414: │  └─ Execute Workflow A
415: │     └─ Expected outcome A
416: ├─ Condition B met
417: │  └─ Execute Workflow B
418: │     └─ Expected outcome B
419: └─ Condition C met
420:    └─ Execute Workflow C
421:       └─ Expected outcome C
422: \```
423: \```
424: 
425: ### Validation Checkpoints
426: 
427: **Purpose**: Named checkpoints throughout workflows
428: 
429: **Format**:
430: ```markdown
431: **Validation**: `checkpoint_name`
432: ```
433: 
434: **Examples**:
435: - `files_analyzed`
436: - `artifacts_filtered`
437: - `strategy_determined`
438: - `root_cause_identified`
439: 
440: **Usage**: Reference in quality checklists and debugging
441: 
442: ### Prerequisites Section
443: 
444: **Purpose**: Link to required standards and context
445: 
446: > **PLACEMENT**: Prerequisites go in **Section 1 OVERVIEW**, NOT in the intro paragraph.
447: 
448: **Format**:
449: ```markdown
450: # [Workflow Name]
451: 
452: [1-2 sentence summary only - no prerequisites here]
453: 
454: ---
455: 
456: \## 1. OVERVIEW
457: 
458: ### Prerequisites
459: Follow [standard name] for all implementations:
460: - **[Standard 1]**: [Brief description]
461: - **[Standard 2]**: [Brief description]
462: - See [standard-file.md](./standard-file.md) for complete requirements
463: ```
464: 
465: **Key Elements**:
466: - Appears in Section 1 OVERVIEW, not intro
467: - Links to other reference files
468: - Lists specific requirements
469: 
470: ### Tool Integration References
471: 
472: **Purpose**: Show MCP tool usage, script execution, asset references
473: 
474: **Format for MCP Tools**:
475: \```markdown
476: **Automated [Task] via MCP:**
477: 
478: Instead of [manual approach], use Chrome DevTools MCP:
479: 
480: \```markdown
481: 1. [Step 1]:
482:    [Use tool: mcp__chrome_devtools__tool_name]
483:    - parameter1: "value"
484:    - parameter2: value
485: 
486: 2. [Step 2]:
487:    [Use tool: mcp__chrome_devtools__tool_name]
488: \```

682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766: 
767: ---
768: 
769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible
882: 
883: ---
884: 
885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```
995: 
996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:
997: ```python
998: def test_quick_mode():
999:     assert route_workflow("$quick fix").mode == "quick"
1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass
1006: 
1007: ---
1008: 
1009: ## 8. STANDARD STRUCTURE TEMPLATE
1010: 
1011: ### Complete Skill Directory Structure
1012: 
1013: **Path:** `.skilled/skills/` (singular, not `skills` or `openskills`)
1014: 
1015: ```
1016: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
1017: ├── SKILL.md                    # Main skill file (Level 2 in progressive disclosure)
1018: ├── references/                 # Deep-dive technical documentation (Level 3)
1019: │   ├── workflow-name.md        # Multi-phase workflows with checkpoints (kebab-case)
1020: │   ├── patterns-library.md     # Before/after code patterns (kebab-case)
1021: │   ├── debugging-guide.md      # Systematic troubleshooting (kebab-case)
1022: │   └── quick-reference.md      # Commands, shortcuts, checklists (kebab-case)
1023: ├── scripts/                    # Executable Python logic
1024: │   ├── mode_detection.py       # Procedural logic, algorithms
1025: │   ├── workflow_router.py      # Decision logic
1026: │   ├── config_validator.py     # Data transformation
1027: │   └── __init__.py             # Package initialization
1028: ├── assets/                     # Configuration and data files
1029: │   ├── workflow-configs/       # YAML workflow definitions
1030: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
1031: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
1032: │   ├── mappings/               # YAML mapping data
1033: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
1034: │   │   └── mode-recognition.yaml
1035: │   └── templates/              # Markdown/code templates
1036: │       ├── template-name.md
1037: │       └── component-template.tsx
1038: └── tests/                      # Unit and integration tests
1039:     ├── test_mode_detection.py
1040:     ├── test_workflow_router.py
1041:     ├── test_config_validator.py
1042:     └── __init__.py
1043: ```
1044: 
1045: ### Directory Purposes
1046: 
1047: **SKILL.md** (Required): Overview, workflow (3-5 steps), rules. Target: <200 lines
1048: 
1049: **references/** (Optional): Detailed workflows, patterns, debugging. Target: 500-3000 lines/file. **All authored filenames must use kebab-case.**
1050: 
1051: **scripts/** (Optional): Python logic - procedural, routing, validation. Requires type hints, tests
1052: 
1053: **assets/** (Optional): YAML configs, workflow definitions, templates, mappings
1054: 
1055: **tests/** (Required if scripts/ exists): Unit tests with ≥80% coverage, pytest, `test_[name].py`
1056: 
1057: ### When to Create Each Directory
1058: 
1059: | Directory     | Create When                                                     | Don't Create When                           |
1060: | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
1061: | `references/` | Content >200 lines, multi-phase workflows, systematic debugging | Simple skills <200 lines total              |
1062: | `scripts/`    | Python logic extracted from markdown, reusable functions        | Pure documentation, no executable logic     |
1063: | `assets/`     | YAML configs, templates, structured data                        | No configuration data, inline examples only |
1064: | `tests/`      | `scripts/` directory exists                                     | No Python scripts to test                   |
1065: 
1066: ### Integration Pattern
1067: 
1068: **How components work together:**
1069: - SKILL.md references scripts: `[workflow_router.py](./scripts/workflow_router.py)`
1070: - Scripts load configs: `yaml.safe_load(f"../assets/config.yaml")`
1071: - Tests verify scripts: `assert route_workflow("input").mode == "expected"`
1072: - Markdown links to all: "See [script.py](../scripts/), [config.yaml](../assets/)"

38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal

68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.

202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?

204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.

682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs

769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:

871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):

873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:

885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown

962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown

969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:

977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass

984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```

996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:

1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass

14: # Hermes MCP Policy
15: 
16: Hermes hosts MCP servers, but only from the operator's configuration. This is a structural difference from every sibling runtime, which registers servers in a repo dotfolder.
17: 
18: ## 1. OVERVIEW
19: 
20: MCP servers reach a Hermes session only from the operator's user-level configuration; this reference records that boundary, the one operator step, the deny-by-default posture and what a dispatch may assume.
21: 
22: ---
23: 
24: ## 2. WHERE MCP LIVES
25: 
26: `mcp_servers:` is read from `~/.hermes/config.yaml` only (source-read: `hermes_cli/mcp_config.py`). `hermes mcp add|remove|list|test|configure` manage it; `hermes tools list|disable|enable` toggle tools with `server:tool` notation. `--safe-mode` disables all MCP servers for a run, and the `chat` path waits for MCP cold start before its first tool snapshot, so a configured server adds startup latency to every dispatch.
27: 
28: ---
29: 
30: ## 3. THE OPERATOR STEP
31: 
32: To reach the repo's code-mode server from Hermes, the operator runs, once:
33: 
34: ```bash
35: printf 'Y\n' | hermes mcp add code_mode --command node --env UTCP_CONFIG_FILE=.utcp_config.json --args .skilled/bin/mcp-code-mode-launcher.cjs
36: hermes mcp list
37: ```
38: 
39: Observed 2026-09-14: `--args` must be the last option, the command connects and discovers seven tools, and the "Enable all tools?" prompt needs an answer on stdin (a closed stdin cancels the add). A dispatch never runs these. A session reaches the server only when its name appears in the `-t` list (`-t search,todo,code_mode`).
40: 
41: ---
42: 
43: ## 4. DENY BY DEFAULT
44: 
45: After adding a server, disable every tool and enable the few a task needs:
46: 
47: ```bash
48: hermes tools disable code_mode
49: hermes tools enable code_mode:search_tools code_mode:call_tool_chain
50: ```
51: 
52: Pre-spawn security filters drop configurations shaped like exfiltration; OAuth device flow covers remote servers. `hermes mcp serve` (Hermes as an MCP server) has no consumer in this repo and is not part of this policy.
53: 
54: ---
55: 
56: ## 5. WHAT A DISPATCH MAY ASSUME
57: 
58: Nothing about MCP unless `hermes mcp list` shows the server. A prompt that needs a tool from a server checks the list first, and stops with a report if the server is absent. The packet's hard rule `mcp-config-operator-required` states this boundary.

4: trigger_phrases:

13: 
14: # Hermes CLI Integration Patterns
15: 
16: How the calling AI integrates Hermes without duplicating the deep-loop executor. The shared runtime owns process construction; this reference never inserts a packet-local shell wrapper between the skill and that runtime.
17: 
18: ## 1. OVERVIEW
19: 
20: ### Core Principle
21: 
22: The calling AI is the conductor; Hermes is the delegated executor. Every pattern below ends with the conductor reading the exit code, stdout and stderr and verifying the result with the command the prompt named.
23: 
24: ---
25: 
26: ## 2. PATTERNS
27: 
28: ### Write dispatch
29: 
30: 1. Probe `command -v hermes` and `hermes config get providers.llmgateway.base_url`.
31: 2. Write the prompt file: preamble, inlined persona, task, exact files, acceptance, verification command.
32: 3. Dispatch with `--yolo`, `--ignore-rules`, `--source tool`, the leaf toolset list, `--run-budget` under your timeout.
33: 4. Read exit code; on 0 read stdout and run the verification command yourself.
34: 5. Diff the paths touched against the paths authorized; anything else goes back out.
35: 
36: ### Read-only review
37: 
38: Same shape without `--yolo`, with `-t file,todo` and `SPECKIT_HERMES_READ_ONLY=1` in the environment so the repo plugin refuses the write tools (the fan-out sets both for a read-only lineage). The prompt asks for findings with `file:line` citations and forbids edits. Open every citation you are about to repeat.
39: 
40: ### Cross-validation
41: 
42: Dispatch the same brief to Hermes on `glm-5.3-flash` and to a sibling runtime (Pi on the same gateway model, or Codex). Compare findings; where they disagree, name what would settle it. Agreement between two runs of the same model is not corroboration.
43: 
44: ### Fan-out lineage
45: 
46: Use `--executor=cli-hermes` on `/deep:research` or `/deep:review`. Set the lineage `timeoutSeconds` to 900 or more: the one live research iteration ran 1042 seconds against a 600-second setting and finished only because the runner's ceiling is twice `iterations × timeoutSeconds` (observed 2026-09-14). A lineage may also name MCP servers in `liveTools.mcpServers`; the builder appends them to `-t`. The runtime builds the command, passes the prompt on stdin, applies write containment to the lineage directory, and treats exit 1 as failure. Keep `iterations × timeoutSeconds` under the four-hour lineage ceiling.
47: 
48: ### Session continuation
49: 
50: Capture `session_id:` from stderr. A follow-up may resume with `hermes chat --resume <id>`, but a dispatch never resumes an operator's interactive session, and the resumed run still passes `--ignore-rules` and an explicit toolset list.
51: 
52: ---
53: 
54: ## 3. ANTI-PATTERNS
55: 
56: | Anti-pattern | Why it fails | Do instead |
57: |---|---|---|
58: | `hermes -z "<prompt>"` for a dispatch | No session id, auto-approves everything, auto-accepts hooks | `chat -Q --oneshot --query-file` |
59: | Omitting `--yolo` on a write task | Ordinary writes still run; a step Hermes flags as dangerous is blocked headless and the leaf reports it | Pass `--yolo` with every write or terminal toolset; never on a read-only run |
60: | Omitting `--ignore-rules` | `SOUL.md`, memories and CWD rules enter the leaf prompt | Always pass it |
61: | Default toolset roster | `delegation` and `memory` are enabled | Explicit `-t` list |
62: | `--worktree` | Writes `.git/worktrees/` inside the repo; containment reverts it | Let the runner own isolation |
63: | Trusting exit 0 alone | A budget-cut partial answer also exits 0 | Verify with the named command |
64: | `hermes import-agent` | Copies repo state into the user home, bypasses trust | Inline personas; use prompt templates |
65: | Relocating `HERMES_HOME` per lineage | A fresh home has no credentials | Shared home plus `--ignore-rules` |
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 4. HANDBACK
70: 
71: Report what ran and what it returned (exit code, stdout head, `session_id:`), what the verification command showed, and which paths changed. A Hermes `COMPLETE` in stdout is a claim about itself until the verification command confirms it.

39:   llmgateway:
40:     base_url: https://api.llmgateway.io/v1
41:     key_env: LLMGATEWAY_API_KEY
42: ```

51: 
52: | Model id | Provider | Reasoning | Standing | Notes |
53: |---|---|---|---|---|
54: | `deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017` | `llmgateway` | pinned `max` | **observed 2026-10-22**: a live fan-out dispatch with no model pinned built `--model deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017` and replied `OK` | The rotation default; the same literal cli-pi dispatches through DevPass |

17: 
18: The single catalog of the models, aliases, defaults, permission-mode lever, and dispatch shapes the cli-devin mode can reach.
19: 
20: ---
21: 
22: ## 1. OVERVIEW
23: 
24: ### Purpose
25: 
26: One place to answer "which model, which uid, which permission mode, how to dispatch" for cli-devin.
27: 
28: ### When to Use
29: - Choosing a `--model <alias>` for a `devin -p` dispatch
30: - Mapping desired autonomy onto the `--permission-mode` lever (Devin has no headless reasoning-effort flag)
31: - Recalling the default model and the canonical non-interactive invocation shape
32: 
33: ### Core Principle
34: 
35: This mode is backed by **Cognition's Devin CLI**, a single binary that fronts 37 model families through family slugs, aliases, and model uids. This catalog curates the families kept in scope for cli-devin: DeepSeek, GLM-5.2, GPT-5.6 (Luna Max only), Grok, and SWE-1.7. Gemini 3.8 Flash High was retired from this route on 2026-09-06 (see the note below).
36: 
37: ### Scope
38: This file enumerates the model/alias/default facts and the dispatch envelope. It does NOT own: the full `devin` flag surface, auth pre-flight, session and troubleshooting tables (see [cli-reference.md](./cli-reference.md)), per-model prompt-craft (see [../SKILL.md](../SKILL.md) §4 Rule 10), or the fan-out / model-enforcement runtime (see §6).
39: 
40: ### Authority pointers
41: - Full CLI flags, subcommands, auth pre-flight, permission modes, troubleshooting → [cli-reference.md](./cli-reference.md)
42: - Dispatch envelope + failure-mode matrix → [integration-patterns.md](./integration-patterns.md)
43: - Live model ids on a given install → `devin models`
44:

48:

# Hermes Agent Delegation Reference

This reference prevents a category error: Hermes profiles and `delegate_task` sub-agents are not persona surfaces for this repo's agents.

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Core Principle

The repo's agents (`.skilled/agents/*.md`, the authored source) reach a Hermes dispatch only inside the prompt. Hermes has no flag that loads an agent file, its profiles are whole-home islands, and `delegate_task` children receive a goal and context, never an agent definition.

---

## 2. PERSONA ROUTES

| Route | Works | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| Inline the persona block at the top of the prompt, after the child-dispatch preamble | Yes | Default; the `cli-codex` and `cli-pi` precedent |
| Persona skill preloaded with `-s <name>` from `./.hermes/skills` | Yes, after the trust grant | Only if prompt size becomes a measured problem; needs the repo-local folder and the operator's trust |
| `hermes profile create` per agent | No | Profiles isolate homes and credentials, not personas |
| `hermes import-agent claude-code` | No | Imports `CLAUDE.md` into memories and copies skills into the user home; never imports agent files; bypasses trust and quarantine |

Resolve the persona from the calling runtime's agent directory (AGENTS.md §9), since Hermes has none of its own and its personas travel inlined in the prompt, and map each subtask to the right agent (code, review, design, deep-research, markdown). The canonical contract is `../../../sk-prompt/assets/cli-prompt-quality-card.md` "Persona Injection".

# Hermes CLI - Complete Command Reference

This reference records the Hermes contract as read from the installed source (v0.21.1, upstream `dc90a75a`, git install at `~/.hermes/hermes-agent`) and from live help output on 2026-09-14. Claims marked **source-read** await the contract pin; the one live observation is marked **observed**.

Sources: [research synthesis](../../../../specs/cli-external-orchestration/071-cli-hermes-creation/001-deep-research/research/research.md), [contract pin](../../../../specs/cli-external-orchestration/071-cli-hermes-creation/002-hermes-contract-pin/implementation-summary.md).

## 1. OVERVIEW

Hermes Agent is a Python agent CLI with a large tool surface (terminal, file, search, web, browser, vision, delegation, memory, skills, MCP) and a provider catalog of some forty providers. The binary is `hermes`; `hermes --version` prints the version, install method and install directory. Record the installed version at execution time.

Hermes has three headless forms, and only one is auditable:

| Form | Invocation | Stdout | Session id | Approvals |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Quiet oneshot chat (**use this**) | `hermes chat -Q --oneshot -q "<prompt>"` or `--query-file <path>` | Final response only | `session_id: <id>` on stderr | Flagged actions blocked; `--yolo` lifts the gate |
| Non-TTY chat | `hermes chat -q "<prompt>"` with stdio not a TTY | Response plus banner and previews unless `-Q` | On stderr | Same as above |
| Top-level oneshot (**never for dispatch**) | `hermes -z "<prompt>"` | Final response only | None | Auto-approves everything and auto-accepts hooks |

---

## 2. FLAGS THAT MATTER FOR DISPATCH

| Flag | Effect | Standing |
|---|---|---|
| `-q, --query TEXT` | The prompt in argv; on a non-TTY it answers and exits | live help |

# Hermes CLI Unique Capabilities

Reference for the Hermes surfaces that differ from `cli-codex`, `cli-claude-code`, `cli-opencode`, `cli-cursor`, `cli-devin` and `cli-pi`. Everything here is source-read on v0.21.1 unless marked observed; the contract pin records the live checks.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Core Principle

Hermes exposes more of its surface through named toolsets and user-level configuration than any sibling, and it reads a repo's `.hermes/` folder for exactly two things: skills and plugins. Knowing which is which decides what a dispatch may rely on and what stays an operator step.

---

## 2. TOOLSETS

`-t LIST` replaces the configured toolset roster for the run. Toolsets relevant to dispatch (from `toolsets.py`):

| Toolset | Carries | Leaf policy |
|---|---|---|
| `terminal` | Shell execution | Included for write leaves |
| `file` | `read_file`, `write_file`, `patch`, `search_files` | Always: it is the only toolset that reads files. A read-only leaf keeps it without `terminal`, and the repo plugin refuses the write tools under `SPECKIT_HERMES_READ_ONLY=1` |
| `search` | `web_search` only (no file search) | Never as a stand-in for file reading; `web` covers it when web search is allowed |
| `skills` | Skill loading and management | Included for write leaves |
| `todo` | Task list | Always |
| `web` | `web_search`, `web_extract` | Per the web-search policy: `live` and `inherit` include it, `disabled` omits it |

# Hermes CLI - Complete Command Reference

This reference records the Hermes contract as read from the installed source (v0.21.1, upstream `dc90a75a`, git install at `~/.hermes/hermes-agent`) and from live help output on 2026-09-14. Claims marked **source-read** await the contract pin; the one live observation is marked **observed**.

Sources: [research synthesis](../../../../specs/cli-external-orchestration/071-cli-hermes-creation/001-deep-research/research/research.md), [contract pin](../../../../specs/cli-external-orchestration/071-cli-hermes-creation/002-hermes-contract-pin/implementation-summary.md).

## 1. OVERVIEW

Hermes Agent is a Python agent CLI with a large tool surface (terminal, file, search, web, browser, vision, delegation, memory, skills, MCP) and a provider catalog of some forty providers. The binary is `hermes`; `hermes --version` prints the version, install method and install directory. Record the installed version at execution time.

Hermes has three headless forms, and only one is auditable:

| Form | Invocation | Stdout | Session id | Approvals |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Quiet oneshot chat (**use this**) | `hermes chat -Q --oneshot -q "<prompt>"` or `--query-file <path>` | Final response only | `session_id: <id>` on stderr | Flagged actions blocked; `--yolo` lifts the gate |
| Non-TTY chat | `hermes chat -q "<prompt>"` with stdio not a TTY | Response plus banner and previews unless `-Q` | On stderr | Same as above |
| Top-level oneshot (**never for dispatch**) | `hermes -z "<prompt>"` | Final response only | None | Auto-approves everything and auto-accepts hooks |

---

| Flag | Effect | Standing |
|---|---|---|
| `-q, --query TEXT` | The prompt in argv; on a non-TTY it answers and exits | live help |

# Hermes CLI Unique Capabilities

Reference for the Hermes surfaces that differ from `cli-codex`, `cli-claude-code`, `cli-opencode`, `cli-cursor`, `cli-devin` and `cli-pi`. Everything here is source-read on v0.21.1 unless marked observed; the contract pin records the live checks.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Core Principle

Hermes exposes more of its surface through named toolsets and user-level configuration than any sibling, and it reads a repo's `.hermes/` folder for exactly two things: skills and plugins. Knowing which is which decides what a dispatch may rely on and what stays an operator step.

---

## 2. TOOLSETS

`-t LIST` replaces the configured toolset roster for the run. Toolsets relevant to dispatch (from `toolsets.py`):

| Toolset | Carries | Leaf policy |
|---|---|---|
| `terminal` | Shell execution | Included for write leaves |
| `file` | `read_file`, `write_file`, `patch`, `search_files` | Always: it is the only toolset that reads files. A read-only leaf keeps it without `terminal`, and the repo plugin refuses the write tools under `SPECKIT_HERMES_READ_ONLY=1` |
| `search` | `web_search` only (no file search) | Never as a stand-in for file reading; `web` covers it when web search is allowed |
| `skills` | Skill loading and management | Included for write leaves |
| `todo` | Task list | Always |
| `web` | `web_search`, `web_extract` | Per the web-search policy: `live` and `inherit` include it, `disabled` omits it |

# OpenCode CLI - Agent Delegation

How cli-opencode routes dispatches to specialized OpenCode agents via the `--agent <slug>` flag. The calling AI decides WHAT to delegate. The agent's frontmatter shapes HOW the dispatched session processes it.

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

OpenCode agents are markdown files under `.opencode/agents/<slug>.md`. Each file's frontmatter pins the model, tool permissions, system prompt, and behavioral constraints. When `opencode run --agent <slug>` is invoked, the dispatched session inherits all of that.

The cli-opencode skill exposes the project's full agent roster. The calling AI selects the right slug based on the task type. The agent then shapes the dispatched session — different model, different tool permissions, different system prompt.

### Discovery commands

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `opencode agent list` | List all registered agent slugs across project + user scopes |
| `opencode debug agent <slug>` | Print resolved frontmatter and system prompt for a slug |
| `opencode debug skill <slug>` | Print skill resolution if the agent loads one |

Project-local agents resolve from `.opencode/agents/<slug>.md`. User-level agents fall back from `~/.opencode/agents/<slug>.md` when the project file is missing. The `debug agent` subcommand prints the merged result so the calling AI can confirm which file the dispatch will load.

### Orchestration principle

The calling AI decides WHAT to delegate. The agent's frontmatter shapes HOW the dispatched session processes the task. The calling AI always validates and integrates the output.

This separation of concerns is load-bearing for the cli-opencode skill: the calling AI owns the task graph and the integration step, while the dispatched OpenCode session owns the per-task execution under the agent's tool permissions and system prompt.

---

## 2. ORCHESTRATION MODEL

```text
Calling AI (CONDUCTOR)
  |
  |-- Analyzes task, selects OpenCode agent slug
  |-- Constructs opencode run command with --agent <slug> flag
  |-- Delegates via Bash tool
  |
  v
opencode run --agent <slug> (EXECUTOR ENTRY)
  |
  |-- Resolves .opencode/agents/<slug>.md frontmatter
  |-- Pins model, tool permissions, system prompt, behavioral rules
  |-- Loads project plugins, skills, and MCP servers
  |
  v
OpenCode Session (AGENT EXECUTION)
  |
  |-- Agent shapes the dispatch under its frontmatter constraints
  |-- Streams JSON events (session.started, message.delta, tool.call,
  |    tool.result, session.completed) to the calling AI
  |-- Honors LEAF agent restrictions (no nested dispatches, read-only)
  |
  v
Calling AI (CONDUCTOR — RESULT HANDBACK)
  |
  |-- Parses the JSON event stream
  |-- Validates agent output quality
  |-- Integrates findings into the parent workflow
  |-- Decides next step (next dispatch, completion, escalation)
```

### Invocation pattern

`--agent <slug>` is valid at the top level ONLY for the primary agent `orchestrate` (and `plan`, an OpenCode built-in) — never for `general` (rejected, omit `--agent` instead) and never for a subagent slug (`context`, `markdown`, `review`, `debug`, `ai-council`) or a command-owned loop executor (`deep-research`, `deep-review`, `deep-improvement`, `prompt-improver`), all of which route through `--agent orchestrate`'s Task-dispatch or their owning `/deep:*` command (§3-4 below). When `--agent orchestrate` IS used, the flag loads the agent definition from `.opencode/agents/orchestrate.md` (project-local) or the user-level fallback. The dispatch shape pins model, variant, format, and working directory alongside the agent slug:

```bash
opencode run \
  --model deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro \
  --agent <slug> \
  --variant high \
  --format json \
  --dir /repo \
  "<prompt>"
```

The `--variant high` flag is the cli-opencode default for cross-AI dispatches. The agent's own frontmatter may override the model selection if the agent pins a specific model. When an agent does NOT pin a model, the `--model` flag wins.

### Conductor rules

1. The calling AI always **decomposes** complex tasks before delegating to a single agent.
2. The calling AI always **validates** OpenCode output before integrating.
3. The calling AI never **blindly forwards** user requests to OpenCode without picking the right agent.
4. OpenCode agents operate within their declared tool-permission boundaries — LEAF agents may not write files or dispatch sub-agents.
5. If an agent returns low-quality output, the calling AI retries with refined instructions or selects a different agent.
6. Each `opencode run` invocation is **stateless** by default — include all necessary context in the prompt or use `--continue` / `--session <id>` for explicit continuation.
7. The calling AI surfaces the JSON event stream to the operator when relevant, especially `tool.call` events.

### Orchestration boundaries

| Concern | Owner |
|---------|-------|
| Task selection and decomposition | Calling AI |
| Agent slug selection | Calling AI |
| Prompt construction (RCAF / TIDD-EC / etc.) | Calling AI |
| Model and variant selection | Calling AI (agent frontmatter may pin) |
| Tool permissions inside the dispatch | Agent frontmatter |
| System prompt and behavioral rules | Agent frontmatter |
| Result validation and integration | Calling AI |
| Memory handback extraction | Calling AI |

# cli-external-orchestration Surface Router — per-mode leaf sets

This is cli-external-orchestration's second-layer (surface) router. The hub
selects a workflow mode in [`hub-router.json`](../../hub-router.json)
(`cli-opencode`, `cli-claude-code`, or `cli-codex`); this doc maps a request's
CLI-dispatch intent to the exact packet-local leaf resources that mode should
load. Every path is packet-qualified (`<packet>/references|assets/…`, where
`<packet>` is the mode's `mode-registry.json` `packet` field) and converts to
the canonical `(workflowMode, leafResourceId)` pair at the one contract boundary
(`sk-doc/create-skill/scripts/lib/leaf-resource-contract.cjs`).

Routing is two stages: the hub picks the WORKFLOW mode (mode telemetry), this
router picks the LEAVES within it. The two layers stay separate — the hub never
emits leaf paths, and this router never re-decides the mode.

---

## 1. INTENT MODEL

- **cli-opencode leaves** — the OpenCode CLI command reference (invocation flags,
  models, sandbox) and the integration-pattern guide a request to dispatch an
  external / parallel-detached OpenCode session, run a full plugin + Spec-Kit
  runtime, or fan out a small-model worker loads.
- **cli-claude-code leaves** — the Claude Code CLI command reference (non-interactive
  `claude -p`, extended thinking, permission modes) and the integration-pattern
  guide a request for an Anthropic-backed second opinion, extended-thinking
  handoff, or surgical structured-output dispatch loads.
- **cli-codex leaves** — the Codex CLI command reference (`codex exec`, sandbox
  modes, web research) and the integration-pattern guide a request to dispatch an
  OpenAI-backed coding / review / research session loads.

A bare CLI-dispatch phrase that names no executor (e.g. "dispatch this to a CLI
executor") names no mode, so it fires no intent and falls back to the hub default
(disambiguation) — the router does not silently default to `cli-opencode` on
genuine ambiguity.

## 3. HOW IT WORKS

### Prerequisites

```bash
# Verify installation (cli-opencode v1.0.0 is pinned to opencode v1.3.17)
opencode --version | grep -q '^1\.' || echo "Not installed or version drift. See references/cli-reference.md §9."

# Self-invocation guard
env | grep -q '^OPENCODE_' && echo "ERROR: Already inside OpenCode session"

# Authentication — providers configured via opencode providers (alias auth)
opencode providers
```

**Authentication options**: `opencode providers login <provider>` (and `opencode auth login` for subscription plans). Full per-provider login shapes and the configured-provider list: `references/cli-reference.md` §4.

### Provider Auth Pre-Flight (Smart Fallback)

**MANDATORY before any first dispatch in a session.** The default provider may not be logged in — silently failing with `provider/model not found` or `401 Unauthorized` mid-dispatch wastes a round-trip. Run the pre-flight once per session, cache the result, and re-run only on an auth failure.

The one-shot pre-flight bash, the per-provider decision trees, the user-facing prompt templates for missing providers, and the error-recovery contract live in [`references/cli-reference.md`](./references/cli-reference.md) §4 — do not duplicate them here. Never substitute a model the user didn't approve; ASK when the default is unavailable.

### Default Invocation (Skill Default)

**Default model + variant + format + dir**: `deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro` · `--variant high` · `--format json` · `--dir <repo-root>` (pinned to avoid CWD ambiguity). Direct DeepSeek is the default provider — elevated reasoning at low cost for routine dispatches.

Use `opencode run --model deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro --variant high --format json --dir <repo-root> "<prompt>"`.

> **The `--agent` flag (read this):** Do NOT pass `--agent` on a top-level `opencode run` — current opencode treats named agents like `general` as **subagents** and rejects them at the top level, so `--agent general` fails outright. The default agent runs when `--agent` is omitted, which is correct for almost every dispatch. **To target a specific agent profile, describe the role in the prompt body instead** (e.g. open with "Act as a code-review agent: …"); only pass `--agent <name>` after confirming acceptance via `opencode run --help` on the installed version.

Honor explicit user model, port, and handback phrasing verbatim; otherwise use the default invocation above.

### Core Invocation Pattern

Core flags: `--model`, `--agent`, `--variant`, `--format json`, `--dir`, continuation/session/fork flags, `--share` and `--port` for detached sessions, `--file`, `--thinking`, `--pure`, and log flags.

> **Non-interactive invocation stdin**: always append `</dev/null` to any non-interactive `opencode run` invocation — without it, opencode can inherit parent-terminal stdin and hang. See `references/integration-patterns.md` §6.

> **Registered command dispatch (`--command`)**: slash-command text inside a `run` message is NOT expanded — `opencode run "/memory:search query"` delivers the slash text as raw prose. Execute a registered command via `opencode run --command <family>/<name> [flags] "<args>"` (becomes `$ARGUMENTS`; e.g. `memory/search` for `/memory:search`). Full semantics: `references/cli-reference.md` §4.

### Model Selection

Run `opencode providers list` to confirm credentials and `opencode models <provider>` for live choices. Default: `deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro --variant high` (direct DeepSeek API). Alternates (all omit `--agent`): MiniMax Token Plan/Direct API `MiniMax-M3`, Xiaomi Token Plan/Direct API `mimo-v2.5-pro` (+ low-latency `-ultraspeed`), Kimi For Coding `k2p7` (256k, subscription), Z.AI GLM Coding Plan `glm-5.2` (1M, subscription), and the OpenAI GPT-5.6 catalog (`gpt-5.6-sol` flagship default; bare/Sol/Terra/Luna x base/Fast/Pro, `--variant` up to `xhigh`). Full model table, per-provider `--variant` mapping, and model-specific operational caveats: `references/cli-reference.md` §5.

Shared small-model facts, context defaults, quota pools, and fallback targets live in `../../sk-prompt/prompt-models/assets/model-profiles.json`.

### OpenCode Agent Delegation

The calling AI is the conductor. OpenCode distinguishes **primary agents** (directly invokable via `--agent <slug>`) from **subagents** (dispatched as Task-tool subagents from a primary).

#### Primary agents — directly invokable via `--agent`

OpenCode defines `general`, `plan`, and `orchestrate` as primary agents. **Never pass `--agent general`** — it is rejected at the top level; the default agent (used when `--agent` is omitted) already covers that case. Pin `--agent plan|orchestrate` only when the task needs that profile AND `opencode run --help` confirms top-level acceptance; otherwise state the role in the prompt body.

#### Subagents — dispatched as Task subagents from a primary

These live at `.opencode/agents/<slug>.md` with `mode: subagent` and are NOT directly invokable via `opencode run --agent`. Three dispatch surfaces are legal under the single-hop NDP contract:

1. **Generic subagents** (`context`, `review`, `write`, `debug`) — dispatched by `orchestrate` via the Task tool. Route through `--agent orchestrate` and let it dispatch the relevant subagent.
2. **`ai-council`** — dispatched via `/deep:ai-council` or `orchestrate`'s registry-backed Task-dispatch. Direct `--agent ai-council` is rejected at the top level (`mode: subagent`).
3. **Command-owned loop executors** (`deep-research`, `deep-review`, `deep-improvement`, `prompt-improver`) — LOOP-OWNED by their parent commands (`/deep:research`, `/deep:review`, `/deep:agent-improvement`, `/prompt`), which own iteration state, convergence detection, and continuity. Never dispatch these directly via raw `--agent <slug>`. `orchestrate` is an authorized **caller/coordinator only** — it may perform exactly one bounded hand-off dispatch to the resolved leaf, but MUST NOT re-implement the loop.

See [agent-delegation.md](./references/agent-delegation.md) for the complete agent roster and dispatch patterns.

### Unique OpenCode Strengths

Full project runtime loading, detached sessions, JSON event streams, agent routing, cross-repo/server dispatch, session continuation, and plugin-disable debugging.

### Essential Commands

Default invocation for external runtime handback; `--share --port <N>` only for explicit detached sessions; `--agent orchestrate` for generic subagent routing; `--dir` for cross-repo dispatch.

### Error Handling


Install missing binaries, refuse ambiguous self-invocation, run provider pre-flight for model/auth errors, check version drift for unknown flags, force `--format json` for empty streams, add `</dev/null` for background loops, confirm `--share`, use `--pure` only for plugin crashes, inspect state logs for stuck sessions.

1. Verify OpenCode CLI is installed before first invocation; confirm version baseline against v1.3.17 (drift handling per `references/cli-reference.md` §9).

Honor user overrides verbatim (e.g. `deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro`, `minimax-coding-plan/MiniMax-M3`, `minimax/MiniMax-M3`, `xiaomi-token-plan-ams/mimo-v2.5-pro`, `xiaomi/mimo-v2.5-pro`, `xiaomi/mimo-v2.5-pro-ultraspeed`, `openai/gpt-5.6-sol-pro`).

5. **Append `</dev/null` to every non-interactive `opencode run` invocation** that redirects stdout and/or stderr to files OR runs inside `while read` loops. opencode v1.14.39 reads stdin at startup before session creation; without explicit closed stdin, automation hangs forever at 0% CPU after the `+60s service=snapshot prune=7.days cleanup` log line.
